conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I’m so glad you’re here; adjusting to life with a baby can be joyful and overwhelming all at once, and your feelings matter.

Today I’d like to complete the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—with you. It’s a short, 10-question form that helps us see how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It screens for symptoms of depression and anxiety that can show up during pregnancy or after birth, and it includes a question about thoughts of self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe.

Everything you share is confidential, and our conversation is a judgment-free zone. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. We’ll move through the questions one by one; each should only take a moment.

Ready to begin?  

First, I’d love to know: over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward with enjoyment to things, or has that felt difficult lately?

It’s… it’s been pretty hard, honestly. Most things I used to like—meeting friends for coffee, even just watching a show—feel kind of flat, like I know I should enjoy them but the feeling isn’t really there. I still try, because I don’t want to disappoint anyone, but it’s like the color’s been drained out.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes a little laugh sneaks out—like when the baby makes a silly face—but it feels forced, and it doesn’t last. Mostly I’m just too tired or worried to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like taking the baby for a walk or having my sister visit—but when the time comes it feels more like a chore I have to get through than something I actually look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby spits up more than usual, or won’t settle, my head jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” I keep replaying every little hiccup and thinking a better mom would’ve prevented it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. Even when everything’s quiet and the baby’s sleeping, I’ll suddenly feel my heart racing—like something awful is about to happen. I check her breathing over and over, or worry the formula isn’t the right temperature, even though I know it’s fine. It’s like my mind won’t turn off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits out of nowhere. Last night I was rocking her in the nursery and suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe—like the walls were closing in. I knew there wasn’t any real danger, but my chest got tight and I had to put her in the crib for a second just so I could sit down and gulp some air. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky the rest of the evening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like I’m drowning in little tasks—dishes, bottles, laundry, feeding, burping—and no sooner do I finish one than another pile appears. I keep telling myself other moms manage, so why can’t I? But the list just keeps looping in my head, and some mornings I can barely get out of bed because I already feel behind.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps replaying everything I think I messed up—did I sterilize the bottles right, was her rash worse, am I already failing her? I finally drift off, but then I jolt awake at every tiny sound she makes, heart pounding, and it takes forever to settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I feel that way most of the day. It’s like a heavy cloud that just sits on me. I’ll watch her smile and know I should feel happy, but the sadness is still right there underneath. Some mornings I wake up already crying and I can’t even explain why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

It’s been… most days this week. Sometimes it’s just quiet tears while I’m nursing, other times I have to put her in the crib for a second because the crying gets so hard I can’t catch my breath. It feels like the sadness just spills out whether I want it to or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

Over the past seven days this new mother has felt overwhelmed by persistent sadness, daily crying, and a sense that even simple tasks are "drowning" her. She tries to enjoy her baby-catching an occasional laugh or smile-but mostly feels emotionally flat, anxious, and guilty, replaying small setbacks as personal failures. She describes sudden panic with chest tightness, near-nightly insomnia driven by racing thoughts, and mornings that begin in tears, yet she remains clear that she wants to feel better and has not harbored any thoughts of harming herself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughs only occasionally and feels forced; clearly diminished enjoyment</sym>, <sym>The mother reports minimal anticipatory joy and describes activities as chores, aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('a lot') and attributes routine infant behaviors to personal failure, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports anxiety "pretty much all the time," with persistent intrusive worries about the baby despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intense, sudden panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) that forced her to stop caring for her baby, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to keep up with daily tasks, ruminating on the to-do list, and struggling to get out of bed—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sleep difficulty on "several nights" with racing thoughts, hypervigilance, and repeated awakenings, semantically matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive sadness "most of the day," waking in tears, and an inability to feel joy even when witnessing the baby's smile, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying "most days this week," which aligns with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Scores on items 1,2,4,5,6,7,8,9 each =3, item 3=3 (self-blame), item 10=0 (no self-harm ideation); total 26/30. Per EPDS guidelines a score ≥14 indicates probable major depression; her score is markedly elevated. She endorses core symptoms of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> (anhedonia, depressed mood most of the day, guilt, insomnia, fatigue/loss of energy, difficulty concentrating implied by overwhelm) plus associated anxiety/panic. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>OB-GYN</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> for formal evaluation and possible medication discussion
2. Request expedited referral to perinatal <med>mental health specialist</med> or psychiatrist for therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and safety planning
3. Encourage immediate support: share results with trusted partner/family so she is not alone with the baby during severe symptoms
4. Promote 15-20 min daily outdoor walks and acceptance of help with housework/overnight feeds to improve sleep and reduce overwhelm
5. Provide 24/7 hotlines (Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773, National Maternal Mental Health line 1-833-943-5746) and local emergency number if feelings worsen
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor response to interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant age not specified)  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [name], LCSW  

Presenting symptoms endorsed (EPDS items paraphrased):
- Marked anhedonia: little genuine enjoyment, activities feel obligatory  
- Persistent low mood, daily crying spells, morning worsening  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Unwarranted, pervasive anxiety and panic attacks (nocturnal, situational)  
- Sleep disruption secondary to intrusive worry, hyper-vigilance about infant safety  
- Overwhelm and sense of “drowning” in routine tasks, self-described as “already behind” on waking  

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days” for at least the past week; functional impact on sleep, caregiving confidence, and basic ADLs.  
No self-harm ideation reported (EPDS item 10 = 0).  

Screening significance: High endorsement of depressive and anxiety items consistent with probable postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety disorder; warrants formal evaluation and safety planning.
